transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hey, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Well, it's kind of a lot, to be honest. I’m here because... well, I just feel like I’m always running hot, you know? Like I've got this motor inside me that I just can't shut off, no matter what I do. 

And it's exhausting, but it's also—well, I've been a firefighter for a while now, and you'd think always being on the go would be a perfect fit for that line of work. You know, hauling heavy gear, dealing with all the adrenaline when the tones drop. But lately, this whole thing has been getting me into trouble at the firehouse. Like, serious trouble. Because even when we're back at the station and supposed to be on standby, or just doing routine maintenance on the rigs, I'm still just entirely wound up. I'm constantly pacing around the bay, I can't just sit in the recliner and watch TV like the rest of the guys. 

The captain actually pulled me aside last week—well, maybe it was two weeks ago, right after that big call on 4th street, the one with the commercial structure fire—and basically told me I need to get this checked out because I'm driving the whole shift up the wall. I just can't seem to power down, ever, and it's really starting to mess with my job.
Do you feel anxious when you're not able to keep moving or doing something?

Anxious? Hmm. I don't know if I'd use the word anxious, exactly. When I hear 'anxious,' I think of, you know, being worried about something, or like your heart is pounding because you're scared of what's going to happen. It's not really like that. 

It's more... well, let me give you an example. We have these mandatory continuing education seminars, right? A couple of weeks ago we had this all-day thing on the new hazardous materials protocols—HazMat ops level stuff, mostly about the updated placards for commercial transport vehicles, which is important, obviously, but dry. Really dry. And we're sitting in this stuffy classroom at the academy, the fluorescent lights are doing that annoying buzzing thing, the instructor is just droning on and on, and I am stuck in this tiny, hard plastic chair. 

I wasn't worried about anything, so I wasn't anxious in that sense, but my skin was just absolutely crawling. It's like this intense, physical pressure building up in my chest and my legs, almost like a coiled spring or a pressure valve that's stuck closed. I just kept bouncing my knee, shifting my weight around, taking my boots off and putting them back on, tapping my pen... I guess I was clicking my pen for like twenty minutes straight without even realizing it, because Martinez—he drives Engine 7, great guy, but he has zero patience—he actually reached over and grabbed the pen right out of my hand and told me to knock it off. 

So, yeah, I wouldn't say I feel anxious, necessarily. I'm not sitting there stressing about my bills or anything. It's just this unbearable, physical need to stand up and do literally anything else. If I'm forced to just sit there and I can't move, I just feel like I'm gonna explode out of my own skin.
Do you feel this intense need to move or do something when you're not at work, like when you're at home or out with friends?

Oh, absolutely. It’s definitely not just a firehouse thing. Honestly, it might actually be worse at home because there’s no structured chaos to hide behind, you know? Like, even on my days off, which you’d think would be my time to just decompress and catch my breath... I just can't do it. 

My wife, she’s always trying to plan these relaxing, quiet family nights for us. Just last Friday, for example, she wanted to do a movie night. We got the popcorn going, the kids picked out some animated movie—I think it was that new Pixar one, or maybe Dreamworks, it doesn't really matter—and we all sit down on the big sectional couch in the living room. It's supposed to be this nice, quiet bonding time. But man, I think I made it maybe ten, fifteen minutes tops before I was already crawling out of my skin again. 

I just have such a hard time doing quiet stuff with my family. If things get too still, I start talking over the movie, just making random comments or pointing out stuff that doesn't make sense, which obviously drives everyone crazy when they're trying to watch. And then I’m shifting around, adjusting the pillows, stretching my legs, and before I know it, I’m getting up. I always tell them I'm just going to the kitchen for a glass of water, but then I wander off. Half the time I end up out in the garage. I'll be out there checking my tools, reorganizing my socket wrenches by size, or making sure the lithium batteries on my power drills are fully charged. 

And then my wife will come out to the garage like an hour later, just standing there in the doorway looking at me like, 'What are you doing? We're supposed to be having family time.' But I just can't sit there for that long. I always end up getting up before I’ve even been sitting long enough to get comfortable. It’s like, if the activity is quiet, I have to fill the silence by talking, or moving, or fixing something. It's really frustrating for them, and honestly, I feel terrible about it because I *want* to be able to just sit and relax with my kids, but my body just won't let me.
Do you have any recurring thoughts that you feel compelled to act on when you're feeling this intense need to move or do something?

Recurring thoughts? Like, some specific idea stuck in my head that I have to act out? No, no, it’s not like that at all. It’s not a thought process. It’s not like I’m sitting there thinking, "Oh, I have to go check the socket wrenches right now or something bad will happen," or "I must stand up and tap my foot three times." It’s not a mental compulsion, if that makes sense. 

It’s purely physical. It’s just this... this raw energy. Like, when I was out in the garage the other night during the movie, I wasn't obsessing over the power drill batteries before I got up. I didn't even know I was going to the garage until I was halfway there. I just knew I couldn't be on that couch for one more second. My legs were twitching, my back felt stiff, my chest felt tight, and my brain was just screaming at me to move. 

It’s almost like... okay, you know when you hold your breath for too long, and your body just takes over and forces you to gasp for air? You aren't thinking, "I need to take a breath because my oxygen saturation is dropping." Your body just does it. That’s what this feels like. It’s a physical reflex. I just have to move, or talk, or do something with my hands, just to bleed off some of that pressure. There’s no specific thought attached to it, no plan, no worry. Just... go. Just move. I don't know if that makes sense, but yeah, it's definitely not a thought thing. It's just my body refusing to stay still.
Are you finding it difficult to maintain relationships with your family or friends due to your inability to sit still or relax?

Yeah, I mean, with my wife, like I was saying about the movie nights, it definitely causes friction. She feels like I don't want to spend time with them, which isn't true, but I get why she feels that way. And my friends are mostly guys from the department anyway, so we're usually doing something active like playing softball or whatever, so they don't notice it as much. 

But honestly? The place where this is really blowing up in my face right now, where it's actually becoming a massive problem, is at work. It’s... it’s actually started costing me trust at the firehouse, which is the worst feeling in the world. In our line of work, if the guys on your crew can't trust you, you've got nothing. You're a liability.

Just a couple of weeks ago, Captain Miller pulled me into his office. And it wasn't just a casual "hey, shut the door, let's chat" kind of thing. It was a formal performance and safety meeting. He had the official forms out, he was taking notes, the whole nine yards. I've been gearing up to take the lieutenant's exam this year—I've got the seniority, I know the job, I've got my associate's degree, and I've been really pushing to move up. But sitting in that office... man, now my shot at moving into leadership feels like it’s just completely slipping away. 

Miller basically told me that the crew feels like they can’t count on me to track the details consistently. Because I'm always pacing, always needing to move on to the next thing, I rush. Like when we're doing morning rig checks. You have to go through every single compartment, check the seals on the SCBA masks, make sure the trauma bags are restocked, test the K-12 saws... it's a lot of standing around looking at clipboards. And because my body is just screaming at me to keep moving, I guess I've been glossing over things just so I can be done standing there. I missed a low cylinder pressure on one of the spare air packs last shift. It didn't cause an incident on the fireground, thank God, but it easily could have. 

And Miller was just like, "If we can't trust you to stand still long enough to properly read a pressure gauge or check an inventory list, how are the guys going to trust you to run a scene as a lieutenant?" So yeah... it's definitely messing up my relationships at home, but the fact that the guys at the station are losing faith in me? That's what's really terrifying me right now. I just can't seem to force myself to slow down and stay still long enough to get the small stuff right.
Are you feeling like your inability to sit still and relax is affecting your overall quality of life?

Yeah, I mean... absolutely. It's affecting everything. Like I said, the stuff at work is what really brought me in here, because being a firefighter, that's my identity, you know? I've been doing this since I was twenty-two, right out of the academy, and the thought of not being able to advance, or worse, being seen as a liability by my own crew... it just eats at me. I've been losing sleep over it, honestly. I'll lie in bed at night, which is already hard enough because my legs are always twitching and I can't get comfortable, and I'll just replay that meeting with Captain Miller over and over in my head. 

And then there's the stuff at home. I mean, my wife is a saint, she really is, but I can see the exhaustion in her eyes. She works too, she's a dental hygienist, so she's on her feet all day, and when she comes home, she just wants peace. And I come in like a tornado because I can't just sit on the couch and ask about her day without getting up to fix a squeaky hinge on the cabinet or pacing around the kitchen island. I can see her getting tense when I start getting restless. It's like my inability to relax makes everyone else around me unable to relax, too. 

And it's not just the big things, it's the little everyday things. Like going out to dinner. We used to love going to this little Italian place downtown, but I can barely make it through the appetizers now without feeling like I need to get up and walk around the block. I end up going to the bathroom three times just to have an excuse to move. It's embarrassing. And I feel like I'm missing out on my own life, you know? Like I'm physically present, but I'm rushing through every moment just to get to the next one, because standing still feels like torture. So yeah, my quality of life is definitely taking a hit. It's just exhausting, being this wired all the time. I just want to be able to sit down, take a breath, and actually be in the moment for once without my body fighting me on it.
Have you ever experienced any repetitive behaviors or mental acts that you feel driven to perform in response to your restlessness?

Wait, isn't that kind of like what we were just talking about a little bit ago? With the recurring thoughts? Because yeah, no, my answer is pretty much exactly the same for that. I really don't have any kind of, like, specific routine or ritual I have to do. It's not like I'm driven to wash my hands a certain number of times or, you know, count the tiles on the floor or repeat a specific phrase in my head to make the jittery feeling go away. 

It's honestly totally random. Like I was saying earlier with the garage and the drill batteries, it's just whatever is in front of me that lets me burn off that physical pressure. Like, just yesterday, I was trying to sit through this online safety module for work—which, by the way, they make us do these web-based trainings now instead of the old hands-on stuff, and sitting at a computer desk staring at a screen is just absolute torture for me. Anyway, I was sitting there, and I ended up completely dismantling my clicky pen. Just took the whole thing apart—the spring, the ink cartridge, the little plastic cap—and then put it all back together. 

But I didn't *have* to take the pen apart, you know? It wasn't some "pen dismantling ritual" that my brain forced me to do to feel safe. If there had been a paperclip on the desk, I would have bent that out of shape instead. If there was a piece of paper, I probably would have folded it or shredded it into a hundred tiny pieces. My hands just needed to be doing something, literally anything, while the guy on the video droned on about hazardous materials protocols. 

So it's never a specific repetitive behavior that I'm driven to do over and over, and definitely no mental acts or counting or anything like that. It's just... general, chaotic movement, I guess. Whatever is handy, whatever gets me out of the chair, whatever keeps my hands busy. I just want to make sure I'm being clear about that, because it's definitely not some kind of organized compulsion. It's just my body needing to do *something* to stop feeling like it's going to crawl out of its own skin.
Did you experience this intense need to move or restlessness when you were a child, before you turned 12?

Oh, man, yeah. Absolutely. It's funny you ask about that age, because I was actually just talking to my mom about this a few weeks ago, right after that awful meeting with my captain. I was venting to her about how I can't seem to just stand still, and she just kind of laughed and sighed at the same time. 

She says I was exactly like this back in grade school, too. I mean, probably even more obvious back then because I didn't have any kind of adult filter or way to hide it. She told me it was just a constant, exhausting struggle from the moment I hit first or second grade. I was always, always the kid who was out of his seat. Like, the teacher would be up at the chalkboard explaining fractions or whatever, and I'd be up at the pencil sharpener for the fifth time, or wandering over to look at the class pet, or just standing by my desk because sitting in that hard little plastic chair felt like absolute torture. My body just rejected it. 

And it wasn't just the moving around, either. I was constantly blurting out answers. If the teacher asked a question and I knew it, I couldn't raise my hand and wait to be called on. I just couldn't physically hold it in. The answer would just shoot out of my mouth before I even realized I was talking. I didn't mean to be disrespectful or disrupt the class, it just... bypassed my brain entirely. 

And the homework... oh man, my poor mom. It was a total nightmare. I was constantly losing my assignments. She would sit down with me at the kitchen table, we'd spend an hour doing a math worksheet, I'd physically put it into my folder, and somehow by the time I got to school the next morning, it was just gone. Vanished. Sucked into a black hole in my backpack. So, of course, the teachers were always sending notes home. My mom kept a whole file of them, I swear, and it was always the exact same story. They'd write, "He's a bright boy, he grasps the concepts, he's smart enough to do the work, but he just won't sit still," or "He needs to learn to stay in his seat and stop interrupting." 

It used to drive my parents crazy because they knew I wasn't stupid, you know? Like, they knew I was bright enough to get straight A's, but I was getting C's and D's on my report card for "citizenship" or "conduct" just because I couldn't sit quietly at a desk for six hours a day. So yeah, this definitely isn't some new thing that just popped up as an adult. It's been my whole life, really. Just this motor running inside me that won't ever shut off, ever since I was a little kid.
Did your parents or teachers ever take you to see a doctor or a specialist about your restlessness and inability to sit still when you were a child?

No, actually... no, they never did. Which, you know, looking back on it now with how much of a struggle it was, you'd think someone would have flagged it and said, 'Hey, maybe he needs to see a pediatrician or something.' But my parents... well, my dad was a mechanic, a real old-school, blue-collar guy, and he just had this mindset that I was just a rowdy boy. He'd always say I just had a motor on me and needed to run it off. 

And the teachers, I mean, they complained constantly, like I said about all those notes my mom kept, but it never really escalated to them suggesting a doctor. It was always framed as a discipline issue, you know? Like, 'he needs to try harder to pay attention,' or 'he needs stricter rules at home.' They just thought I was being difficult on purpose or acting out. 

Plus, I mean, this was the early nineties. I feel like back then, at least in my neighborhood, people weren't as quick to take their kids to specialists for that kind of stuff. If you were bouncing off the walls, they just told you to go outside and play until the streetlights came on. So my mom's solution was just trying to tire me out physically. She'd sign me up for every sport she could find—baseball, soccer, whatever—just hoping I'd crash at the end of the day. But the thing is, I never really crashed. I'd come home from a two-hour soccer practice and still be pacing around the living room or doing laps around the coffee table while we watched TV. 

So yeah, no doctors or specialists back then. Just a lot of parent-teacher conferences and... well, a lot of groundings. I spent so much time grounded in my room, which, let me tell you, is absolute torture for a kid who physically cannot sit still. I'd just end up taking apart my alarm clock or bouncing a tennis ball against the wall for hours until my dad would yell up the stairs for me to knock it off. But yeah, no one ever thought to actually take me to a doctor for it.
Did you exhibit these restless behaviors before the age of 12?

Wait, didn't I just... I mean, I know I talk a mile a minute, so maybe I completely buried the lead in all my rambling earlier, but yeah, like I was saying just a couple of minutes ago, absolutely. Way before I was 12. 

My mom and I were just talking about it, and she says I was exactly like this back in grade school, too. I was always the kid who was out of his seat, wandering around the classroom when I was supposed to be doing desk work. And the blurting out answers—that was a huge one, just totally unable to keep my mouth shut and raise my hand when I knew the answer. Plus, you know, constantly losing my homework in my backpack even though my mom and I had just done it at the kitchen table the night before. 

She actually kept all those notes the teachers sent home over the years in this old file folder, and it was always the exact same story from every single teacher—that I was bright enough to do the work and grasped the concepts, but I just couldn't sit still or stay quiet. So, yeah, I definitely exhibited all of this stuff when I was really little. It wasn't just a teenager thing or an adult thing. It was first grade, second grade, all of it. I mean, I could probably call my mom right now and she'd talk your ear off for an hour about how exhausted I made her before I even hit middle school. So, yes, definitely before age 12.
Have you experienced these restless behaviors in multiple settings, such as at work, at home, and in social situations?

I mean, I don't really... I'm not sure how to answer that, honestly. Because, well, I don't really break my life down into categories like that, you know? Like work, home, social... it all just kind of bleeds together for me, so I haven't really noticed if it's happening in every single one of those specific places. 

Like, at work, at the firehouse, we're always doing something anyway. You're checking the rig, you're cooking dinner for the crew, you're working out, or you're out on a call. It's a 24-hour shift, so there's not a lot of just sitting around to begin with. I mean, sure, sometimes we're in the day room watching a game, and I'm usually the one getting up to check on the food or grabbing people drinks or just kind of standing in the back of the room instead of taking a recliner, but... is that me being restless, or is that just me being a firefighter? I don't really know. It's just how we are. 

And then at home... I live by myself right now, so it's not like I have a wife or kids pointing out that I'm pacing the floors or whatever. I just do my own thing. I'll be home on my off days and I'll start fixing a leaky faucet, then I'll end up out in the driveway washing my truck, and then I'm reorganizing the garage. I'm always moving, but I don't know if I feel that same trapped, intense need to move like I did when I was a kid forced to sit at a school desk, because nobody's forcing me to sit still now. I just do what I want. 

And socially... I mean, mostly I just hang out with the guys from the station anyway. We'll go to a buddy's house for a barbecue, and I'm usually the guy manning the grill or playing cornhole or throwing a football around with their kids. I'm not really sitting still there either, but nobody really cares if you're up and about at a cookout, you know? 

So I guess... I just haven't really tracked it like that. I haven't really noticed if it's a specific problem across all those different settings because my life is just kind of built around being active anyway. I don't know if that's what you mean by multiple settings, but yeah, I don't really have a clear-cut yes or no for you on that one.
Did you often interrupt others or blurt out answers before they finished speaking when you were a child?

Oh, man, yeah. I mean, I know I brought up the whole blurting out answers in grade school thing just a couple of minutes ago, so yeah, definitely as a kid. I just couldn't hold it in. But honestly, it never really went away. It's actually a huge issue for me right now, even as an adult, especially at the firehouse. 

Like, we'll be sitting around the kitchen table or standing by the rig, and the lieutenant or some of the senior guys will be talking through a tactical plan for a drill. Or maybe they're going over how we're going to approach a specific type of call—like, say, a multi-vehicle pileup on the interstate, which we get a lot of because of the big junction just south of our district. And they'll be right in the middle of explaining the staging, or figuring out who's grabbing the extrication tools and who's pulling the first line, and I just... I cut in. I completely interrupt them right in the middle of a sentence because the answer or the next step is already in my head, and it just shoots out of my mouth before I can even hit the brakes. 

It's like my brain is moving five steps ahead—or at least I think it is—and I just physically cannot wait for them to finish getting the words out. And then, you know, a second later I look around the room and realize I just totally stepped on somebody, usually someone with way more time on the job than me, and I completely messed up the flow of the discussion. It always makes me look like a jerk, or like I'm a know-it-all who isn't respecting the chain of command, which isn't it at all. I respect those guys to death, I really do. I just get this intense pressure when I know what's coming next, or when I see the solution they're building toward, and I just blurt it out. It's incredibly frustrating because I'll literally tell myself before a briefing, 'Okay, just listen this time, keep your mouth shut, let the captain speak,' but then someone starts talking and boom, I'm doing it again before I even realize my mouth is open. So, yeah, it was a problem when I was seven, and it's still getting me in trouble at thirty-seven.
Did you often act without much thought to the consequences when you were a child?

Man, that's a tough one to answer. I’m really trying to think back to when I was little—like, you know, elementary school or junior high—and I honestly just don't know if I can say yes or no to that. I don't really have a clear memory of, like, doing things completely blind to what the fallout would be. 

I mean, I know I was a handful, obviously, with the not sitting still and the blurting things out that we just talked about, but as far as just acting without thinking about the consequences... I'm really not sure. My mom was actually pretty strict, so consequences were a very real, very present thing in our house. She had this whole system, like a chore chart on the side of the fridge, and if you stepped out of line or didn't do your part, you knew exactly what was coming. You were grounded, or you lost TV time, or you were stuck pulling weeds in the backyard all weekend. So I feel like I always kind of knew there was a penalty for messing up, you know? Like, I wasn't totally oblivious to the fact that actions have reactions. 

But did I still do dumb stuff anyway? Probably. I mean, I was a kid. Kids do dumb stuff. My brother and I used to build these incredibly sketchy bike ramps out of scrap plywood and cinderblocks we found in the alley behind our subdivision, and looking back, yeah, someone could have easily broken a collarbone. But I don't know if that was me acting without thought to the consequences, or if that was just us being bored boys in the suburbs in the nineties trying to copy what we saw on TV. 

So, yeah, I really don't have a good answer for you on that one. It just doesn't stand out in my mind the same way the talking and the wandering around the classroom do. I might have, but I really just haven't noticed or remembered it being a specific issue like that.
Can you tell me if you've experienced these restless behaviors and difficulties with sitting still in at least two different settings, such as at work and at home?

I mean, I feel like we kind of just touched on this a few minutes ago, right? Because honestly, I don't think I have a better answer for you now than I did then. I really just don't know how to separate it out into different settings like that, because my whole life is just... it's just constant motion, no matter where I am. 

Like I was saying before about the firehouse and being at home, I just don't have a solid yes or no for you. If you're asking if I'm always on the go in both places, then yeah, absolutely. At work, I'm checking equipment, running calls, pacing around the day room. And then at home, I'm exactly the same way. I'll get off a 24-hour shift, come home, and instead of crashing on the couch like a normal person, I'm instantly out in the garage. Like just last week, I completely tore apart the carburetor on my lawnmower because it was running a little rich, and then before I even put that back together, I was up on a ladder cleaning the gutters out because I saw some leaves sticking out. 

So I am definitely always moving at work, and I am definitely always moving at home. But do I have *difficulty* sitting still in both places? I just don't know, because I'm never actually trying to sit still in the first place! Nobody is making me sit at a desk or in a chair for eight hours a day. If I want to get up, I get up. If I want to go fix something, I go fix it. I don't really put myself in situations where I have to force myself to stay seated, so I haven't really noticed if I have a hard time with it, you know? It's just hard for me to look at it as a specific problem across different settings when my entire lifestyle is just built around never really sitting down anyway. So yeah, I'm really just not sure.
Have you been experiencing these restless behaviors and difficulties with sitting still for more than 6 months?

Oh, yeah, definitely more than six months. I'd say... well, if I really track it back, it's been a real, noticeable problem for right about a year and five months. I know the exact timeline because that’s when the department completely overhauled our schedule and our responsibilities at the house. 

See, about a year and five months ago, they bumped us to these longer rotating shifts. It used to be a pretty standard rotation, but now we're doing these extended blocks where you're on for way longer, and it just completely messes with your internal clock and your downtime, you know? But the real kicker—and the reason I think the restlessness has become such a huge issue lately—is that on top of the longer shifts, they dumped a mountain of extra documentation on us. 

Every single call now, even if it's just a basic lift assist or a faulty smoke detector at a nursing home, requires this insanely detailed narrative report in the new software system the city bought. So instead of just washing the rig, restocking the jump bag, and moving on, I'm stuck staring at a computer screen in the watch room. And man, that is when I feel it the absolute most. I literally cannot keep my legs from bouncing, I'm getting up to get coffee four times during one report, I'm pacing out into the apparatus bay and coming back... it's brutal. I just can't sit there and type it out.

And then, right around that exact same time, the battalion chief decided to implement a drone program for scene size-ups on major fires and hazmat calls, and somehow I got tapped for the drone duties. Which sounds cool, right? Flying a drone. But what it actually means is standing completely still in one spot, staring at a tiny little tablet screen, trying to make these tiny little micro-adjustments with my thumbs while the rest of the guys are actually running around doing the physical work. I just want to jump out of my skin when I have to do it. My feet just want to move. 

So, yeah, I mean, I've always been a high-energy guy, but as far as the restlessness being a *real* problem where it's actually getting in the way and making me miserable? Exactly a year and five months, right when all those longer shifts and the extra documentation and the drone duties got added to my plate. It’s just... it’s been driving me absolutely crazy having to actually try and stay still for all that.
Have you been experiencing these restless behaviors for at least 6 months?

Wait, didn't you literally just ask me that? I feel like I'm having déjà vu here, Doc. You just asked if it was more than six months, and I gave you that whole breakdown about it being exactly a year and five months, so... yeah, definitely at least six months. 

I don't know if you're just reading off a strict checklist or a questionnaire or something, which, hey, I totally get if you are. Bureaucracy is bureaucracy. Like I was just saying with that new software system the city forced on us for the fire reports, it actually makes you click the exact same checkboxes three different times on three different screens before you can even hit submit. It's like, "Yes, the patient was breathing," "Yes, respirations were present," "Yes, airway was clear." It drives you absolutely up the wall when you're just trying to get the paperwork done and your legs are bouncing under the desk. So if you're stuck using some redundant medical system like that on your computer right now, I totally sympathize, man. 

But yeah, as far as the restlessness goes, I really don't have any other timeline to give you. I don't know what else to tell you besides what I just laid out with the schedule changes and the drone duty. I haven't noticed it being a specific issue before that whole year-and-five-months mark, so I'm not really sure what else you're looking for with that question.
Have you been experiencing these restless behaviors consistently over the past 6 months?

Okay, Doc, I... I really feel like we are going in circles here. I mean, I know I just said I get that you might be dealing with some clunky checklist system, but are you actually listening to what I'm saying? Because I feel like I've answered this exact same question three times in a row now. 

Yes. Consistently. Absolutely consistently for the past six months, because, like I said, it’s been a real, constant problem for about a year and five months. Ever since the department threw all that new stuff at us. The longer rotating shifts, the mountain of extra documentation on that awful new software, the drone duties where I have to stand completely still... all of that started a year and five months ago, and it hasn't stopped. So yes, the restlessness has been there, consistently, every single shift, every single day, for that entire time. 

I mean, I don't know how else to explain it. The schedule hasn't changed back, the reports haven't gotten any shorter, and the battalion chief hasn't stopped calling for the drone on every major incident. So my legs haven't stopped bouncing, and I haven't stopped pacing out into the apparatus bay when I'm supposed to be typing. It's every day. It's every shift. It's completely consistent.
